author: A Robot
objectives: Identify and name the four heart chambers, four valves, and major vessels entering/leaving the heart.
Trace the step-by-step dual-loop pathway of blood through the heart and distinguish pulmonary vs systemic circuits.
Explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle in terms of required pressure and resistance.
Describe valve function (atrioventricular vs semilunar) and how open/closed states prevent backflow during the cardiac cycle.
Interpret clinical/anatomical terminology, including the dual naming of the mitral/bicuspid valve.

modules.description: Two side-by-side heart models appear: an exterior view with major vessels and a cutaway view showing the four chambers and four valves. Students can rotate both together and use labels to interpret patient vs viewer right-left.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recognize the anatomical orientation of the heart (apex down, slightly left).
Differentiate right vs left heart structures from patient perspective.
Locate major vessels entering and leaving the heart (SVC/IVC, pulmonary trunk/arteries, pulmonary veins, aorta).
instructions: Locate the apex (down and slightly left).
Confirm which side is patient’s right using the on-screen orientation labels.
Use the labels to map exterior vessel landmarks to interior anatomy.

clips.changeMeaning: Shows both heart models and enables right/left orientation labels so students start with correct patient-perspective mapping.
clips.narration: Welcome! This lab uses two views of the heart: an exterior model with major vessels and a cutaway model showing chambers and valves. Keep in mind we describe anatomy from the patient’s perspective.

clips.changeMeaning: Applies a subtle rotation cue to help learners locate the apex direction in 3D space.
clips.narration: First, locate the apex—pointing down and slightly to the left. Use the orientation labels to identify the patient’s right side.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves labels closer to the models to reduce head movement while students scan the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
clips.narration: Now focus on the exterior major vessels: superior and inferior vena cava enter; pulmonary trunk/arteries and pulmonary veins plus the aorta leave.

modules.description: Guided structural tour highlighting the cutaway label in sequence while students map each region to the intact heart.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Name the four chambers in order: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle.
Name the four valves and their between-structures roles.
Match the major vessels in order for later path tracing.
instructions: Follow the label order exactly.
Use the intact heart to connect each highlighted interior structure to an exterior landmark.
Remember mitral/bicuspid dual naming when it appears.

clips.changeMeaning: Activates the tour label and enables an orbiting highlight marker to cue the first structure.
clips.narration: Scene 2 is a structural tour: we’ll start with chambers—right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, then left ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Updates the label to show the tricuspid valve as the atrioventricular connection between right atrium and right ventricle.
clips.narration: Next is the tricuspid valve, the atrioventricular valve between the right atrium and right ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Shows the dual naming (mitral/bicuspid) and continues into the aortic valve and aorta to complete valve-to-vessel mapping.
clips.narration: Now the mitral valve—also called the bicuspid valve. Then the aortic valve and the aorta.

clips.changeMeaning: Consolidates the major-vessel order into a single final label so students can follow it during the blood-flow trace.
clips.narration: Finish with the vessel order you’ll use later: superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins, and the aorta.

modules.description: Cutaway heart with continuously rotating blue and red flow tubes. Labels emphasize pulmonary vs systemic circuits.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Differentiate pulmonary vs systemic circulation using blue/red color mapping.
Explain functional roles of right vs left heart.
Summarize the steady-state circulation pattern through both loops.
instructions: Observe blue vs red for deoxygenated vs oxygenated blood.
Watch the circuit emphasis: pulmonary then systemic.
Use labels to confirm where each loop sends blood.

clips.changeMeaning: Turns on both color-coded flow tubes and circuit labels to establish the dual-circuit visual framework.
clips.narration: At steady state: blue represents deoxygenated blood on the right side heading to the lungs. Red represents oxygenated blood on the left side heading to the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Emphasizes pulmonary circuit label by full opacity and dims systemic label to focus attention on the first loop.
clips.narration: Watch the pulmonary circuit: blood leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary arteries, reaches the lungs, then returns oxygenated via pulmonary veins to the left atrium.

clips.changeMeaning: Emphasizes systemic circuit label after the pulmonary loop, clearly separating the two loops as distinct functional units.
clips.narration: Now the systemic circuit: oxygenated blood exits the left ventricle through the aortic valve into the aorta and supplies the entire body, then returns deoxygenated to the heart via the venae cavae.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4 — Step-by-Step Blood Cell Trace (Next Control)
modules.description: Interactive step trace with a single blood-cell marker moving through the full dual-loop sequence. Label updates at each step.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the ordered path: right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary trunk/arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → systemic return.
Identify where oxygenation changes occur (lung capillaries).
Connect oxygenation in lungs to directionality back to the left heart.
instructions: Use Next to move the blood cell one structure at a time.
Read the structure label each step.
Notice the color change when the cell reaches lung capillaries.

components.text: Press Next to move the blood cell

clips.changeMeaning: Initial placement at SVC with blue color to represent deoxygenated blood and sets the first label.
clips.narration: We begin in the superior vena cava. This blood is deoxygenated—so it’s blue.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the tracer into right atrium and updates the label to include passage through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
clips.narration: The right atrium contracts, pushing blood through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Advances toward pulmonary outflow and updates the label emphasizing pulmonary valve passage into the pulmonary trunk/arteries.
clips.narration: The right ventricle contracts. Blood passes through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the tracer to the lung capillaries and switches from blue to red to indicate oxygenation.
clips.narration: In the lung capillaries, blood picks up oxygen—so the cell turns red.

clips.changeMeaning: Transitions the tracer through pulmonary veins and mitral into the left ventricle, approaching the aortic valve.
clips.narration: Oxygenated blood returns via pulmonary veins to the left side, passes through the mitral valve into the left ventricle, and approaches the aortic valve.

clips.changeMeaning: Completes the loop by updating the label to systemic outflow and return back to the vena cava region.
clips.narration: The left ventricle ejects blood through the aortic valve into the aorta. Blood returns via systemic veins back to the SVC, completing the loop.

modules.description: Side-by-side cross-sections compare right vs left ventricular myocardium thickness at the same level with scale markers.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Visually compare RV vs LV wall thickness using labels and scale markers.
Explain why LV is thicker based on higher systemic pressure/resistance.
Relate wall thickness to required pressure generation for effective perfusion.
instructions: Rotate the cross-sections together to compare thickness.
Mentally estimate the thickness ratio (LV vs RV).
Explain which ventricle needs higher pressure and why.

clips.changeMeaning: Displays both cross-sections and thickness labels with scale markers ready for comparison.
clips.narration: Scene 5 highlights ventricular wall thickness asymmetry: the left ventricle is much thicker than the right.

clips.changeMeaning: Slightly enlarges cross-sections to aid visual confirmation of the approximate three-to-one thickness ratio.
clips.narration: Compare thickness directly: the right ventricle is relatively thin; the left ventricle is about three times as thick.

clips.changeMeaning: Replaces the LV label text to explicitly connect thickness with the higher pressure needed for systemic perfusion.
clips.narration: Why? The left ventricle must pump against much higher resistance to perfuse the entire body.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6 — Valve Function and Prevention of Backflow (Open/Closed States)
modules.description: Valve open/closed state swapping for ventricular contraction vs relaxation. AV valves vs semilunar valves demonstrate backflow prevention.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish atrioventricular vs semilunar valves based on location and function.
Explain open/closed state timing during ventricular contraction vs relaxation.
Identify which valves are open/closed in each phase.
instructions: Observe the open vs closed valve models.
Note category: AV valves (tricuspid, mitral) vs semilunar valves (pulmonary, aortic).
Match valve state to phase of the cardiac cycle.

components.text: Ventricular contraction:\nAV valves closed, Semilunar valves open

clips.changeMeaning: Models ventricular contraction: AV valves closed and semilunar valves open, preventing backflow into the atria.
clips.narration: During ventricular contraction, atrioventricular valves are closed to stop backflow into the atria, while semilunar valves are open so blood can exit the ventricles.

clips.changeMeaning: Models ventricular relaxation: AV valves open and semilunar valves closed, preventing backflow into ventricles.
clips.narration: During ventricular relaxation, AV valves open so blood can fill the ventricles, while semilunar valves close to prevent backflow into the ventricles.

clips.changeMeaning: Replaces the phase-specific message with a unifying conceptual takeaway about one-way valve function.
clips.narration: Think of valves as one-way doors: they open when forward flow is needed and close to stop backflow.

modules.description: Quiz highlighting one structure in the cutaway heart with multiple choice candidate names.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the four chambers from visual highlight.
Identify the four valves (tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral/bicuspid, aortic).
Differentiate pulmonary arteries vs pulmonary veins.
instructions: Select the correct name from the answer choices.
If unsure, compare the highlighted location to known chamber/valve/vessel positions from earlier scenes.
Replay to reinforce recall.

clips.changeMeaning: Starts the quiz with a right atrium highlight and presents multiple chamber options.
clips.narration: Quiz time! Which chamber is highlighted? Choose the correct option.

clips.changeMeaning: Updates the highlight and prompt for a tricuspid valve identification question.
clips.narration: Next: which valve is highlighted? The tricuspid valve separates the right atrium and right ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Tests mitral/bicuspid recognition using a valve highlight and dual naming options.
clips.narration: Which valve is highlighted? Remember: the mitral valve is also called the bicuspid valve.

clips.changeMeaning: Ends quiz with a pulmonary vessel question to reinforce arteries vs veins distinction.
clips.narration: Finally, which vessel is highlighted? Use direction and oxygenation: pulmonary arteries go to lungs; pulmonary veins return to the heart.

modules.moduleName: Scene 8 — Blood Flow Tracing Quiz (Sequence + Direction)
modules.description: Sequence quiz: a marker indicates the current step. Students select the next structure, testing both order and pulmonary vs systemic directionality.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Select correct next structure in the sequence.
Differentiate pulmonary arteries vs pulmonary veins from the direction of blood flow.
Maintain the full loop logic from right atrium → lungs → left heart → body → return.
instructions: Choose the next structure in the path.
If incorrect, focus on whether the next step is toward lungs (pulmonary arteries) or back to heart (pulmonary veins).
Continue until the loop logic completes.

components.text: What is the next structure in the blood path?
Reminder: Pulmonary arteries → lungs; pulmonary veins → heart

clips.changeMeaning: Sets starting position at right atrium and asks for the next structure, reinforcing AV valve ordering.
clips.narration: Start at the right atrium. What comes next in the path? Choose the correct structure.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves marker to right ventricle and tests next-step outflow through the pulmonary valve.
clips.narration: Now you’re at the right ventricle. What’s the next structure as blood leaves the ventricle?

clips.changeMeaning: Targets pulmonary artery vs vein confusion by asking which vessel returns oxygenated blood after lung oxygenation.
clips.narration: After the lungs, which vessel returns blood to the heart? Choose pulmonary veins.

clips.changeMeaning: Completes the systemic direction test by selecting the aorta as the vessel that sends oxygenated blood to the body.
clips.narration: To send oxygenated blood out to the entire body, the next vessel is the aorta.

modules.moduleName: Scene 9 — Recap: Structural Inventory + Dual Circulation
modules.description: Closing recap in AR: recap themes cycle while one highlight marker pulses on the heart model.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Synthesize the structural inventory: chambers, valves, and major vessels.
Connect valve function to prevention of backflow and unidirectional flow.
Summarize dual-circuit organization: pulmonary vs systemic.
Relate LV vs RV wall thickness to pressure/resistance demands.
Recall the full stepwise blood path through the loop.
instructions: Watch the recap highlight move through the five concept areas.
Listen for each concept theme and map it back to earlier scenes.
Use the quiz again if needed for reinforcement.

clips.changeMeaning: Enables recap highlight near the heart center and displays theme 1 to review the structural inventory.
clips.narration: Recap theme one: the structural inventory—four chambers, four valves, and major vessels entering and leaving the heart.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves recap highlight to emphasize pulmonary vs systemic circuit organization and updates the on-screen theme text.
clips.narration: Theme two: dual organization. The pulmonary circuit sends blood to the lungs and returns it to the left heart; the systemic circuit supplies the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights mid-heart regions and displays theme 3 to reinforce the complete step-by-step blood path.
clips.narration: Theme three: the full path of blood—from right atrium through valves and vessels, through the lungs for oxygenation, then through the left heart and out to systemic circulation.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the highlight toward the LV region and updates theme 4 for functional explanation of thickness asymmetry.
clips.narration: Theme four: wall thickness asymmetry. The left ventricle is thicker because it must generate higher pressure to perfuse the entire body.

clips.changeMeaning: Concludes recap with the key functional concept: valve open/closed timing prevents backflow and keeps flow unidirectional.
clips.narration: Theme five: valve function. Atrioventricular valves and semilunar valves open and close at the right times to prevent backflow and keep circulation unidirectional.
